details: A flaky test is a bug (quality-gate rule); it turned the stale-texts gate red on a change that touches none of the gate code, and cost a fix round.
failing_case: Gate of wt/stale-texts, inert probe step: library tests failed on test_f2_an_interrupted_runner_leaves_no_gate_command; fixer saw 3 of 3 passes alone and 0 of 12 under 4 busy loops, so p is below 1/15 and unmeasured.
pass_cases: The race in the gate's SIGINT handling (or in the test's wait) is named with evidence and fixed at the cause.
max(20, ceil(3/p)) clean runs of the test under load after the fix.
reason: tests/test_gate_stops.py:85 passes at head, fails at 7a1a1a9^ (AssertionError, sleep alive).
findings.summary: Gate stop test sometimes sees the gate command alive

details: Introduction for the owner: the gate-stop test F2 failed once in a gate run (the gate's command was still alive after its runner was
interrupted). The project rule for flaky tests says: reproduce the flake under load, measure its failure rate p, then prove the fix
with max(20, 3/p) clean runs under the same load. Here the flake would not reproduce: the fixer saw 0 of 15, I saw 0 of 40 on the old
code. The fixer found a real window instead (a Ctrl-C that lands while Python's Popen is still returning orphans the command) and
proved it with a test that sends the signal inside that window on purpose: the old code fails it every time, the new code passes.
The link from that window to the one failure seen on 27 Oct is reasoning, not a measurement (it is the most plausible cause I found;
the other one I tested, two stops landing together, does not orphan the command).
Question: is the injected reproduction enough proof to merge?
(a) yes: merge now, note in the queue item that p was measured with injection (recommended; more runs of F2 prove nothing at this p).
(b) no: before the merge, a fixer builds a load that makes F2 itself fail on the old code and runs the count the rule asks.
PLAUSIBLE that the window is the 27 Oct cause; CONFIRMED that the window exists and is closed. Size: (a) 5, (b) 60.
evidence: relay queue show gate-stop-test-sometimes-sees-the-gate-command-a: "fixer saw 3 of 3 passes alone and 0 of 12 under 4 busy loops,
so p is below 1/15 and unmeasured"; fixer report: "20/20 clean runs of the file".
measure.sh, 40 runs each, concurrently, ambient load avg 11.7 on 12 cores + 6 busy loops: master "runs 40 failed 0", HEAD "runs 40 failed 0".
F3 copied to a worktree at master: "test_gate_stops.py:119: AssertionError ... 1 failed in 32.32s"; at HEAD "3 passed in 5.23s".
failing_case: Queue item pass case 2: max(20, ceil(3/p)) clean runs of test_f2 under load after the fix. Before the fix the fixer saw 0 failures in
15 runs (p < 1/15, unmeasured), so 3/p >= 45; the fixer reports 20/20 clean runs of the file, load not stated. My 40 runs of F2 on
master and 40 on HEAD under the same load were all clean: the runs cannot tell the fixed code from the unfixed one.
fix_hint: Owner's word; for (a) one line in the queue item's notes naming the injected proof.
pass_cases: Either (a) owner accepts the injected reproduction as the measured p: F3 fails 1 of 1 at master (p = 1 under injection), passes 20 of
20 at HEAD; recorded in the queue item's notes as the proof.
Or (b) F2's own failure is reproduced under a named load on master (p measured, e.g. k failures of n), then ceil(3/p) clean runs of F2
on HEAD under that same load are recorded.
In both: test_f3 at master fails at tests/test_gate_stops.py:119; at HEAD it passes.
reason: Option (a): injected proof recorded in the queue item notes (earlier check); test at :85 fails at base, passes at head.
findings.summary: the flake was never reproduced, so the queue item's proof (max(20, 3/p) clean runs of F2 under load) cannot be met; the fix rests on an injected reproduction

details: CONFIRMED by reading lines 339-346: the re-raise sits after the try/finally, so only a Popen that returns reaches it. The window is
microseconds wide, so this is rare; the cost is a committed red log for a gate that was told to stop. Size: 5.
evidence: lib/relay_gate.py:339-346: held, release = hold_stops(); try: proc = subprocess.Popen(...) finally: release(); if held: os.kill(...)
failing_case: The gate command cannot start (kit.toml names a file that is not executable) and SIGTERM lands while Popen runs. Popen raises
OSError, release() runs in the finally, `if held:` is skipped because the exception propagates, the except OSError branch writes
"could not start", and the gate commits a log with exit 127 and returns 127. Before the change it left at once with SystemExit(143)
and committed nothing. It should still stop (143, no log).
fix_hint: Re-raise inside the finally, after release(): `finally: release(); if held: os.kill(os.getpid(), held[0])`.
pass_cases: SIGTERM held during a Popen that raises OSError: the gate exits 143 and commits no log.
No signal, command not executable: exit 127, log "gate command could not start" committed (as today).
SIGINT held during a Popen that succeeds: KeyboardInterrupt, the command's group killed (test_f3).
findings.summary: a stop held while Popen raises OSError is dropped: the gate goes on to commit a 127 log instead of stopping

details: CONFIRMED with a scratch script. No relay code sends SIGINT to the command's own session today, so nothing breaks now; it is a silent
change of what the command inherits. Size: 5.
evidence: python3 -I -c '... signal.signal(SIGINT, SIG_IGN); subprocess.run(child); held, release = relay_gate.hold_stops(); subprocess.run(child)'
failing_case: `relay gate` started as a background job (`sh -c 'relay gate &'`, SIGINT ignored). Before: the gate command (bin/ci and its tests)
inherited SIGINT ignored. Now: hold_stops installs a Python handler, exec resets a caught signal to default, so the command starts
with SIGINT at default. Measured: a child started under the hold prints default_int_handler, one started without prints 1 (SIG_IGN).
It should inherit the disposition the gate had before the hold.
fix_hint: In hold_stops skip a signal whose handler is SIG_IGN: `if signal.getsignal(sig) == signal.SIG_IGN: continue` (an ignored stop needs no hold).
pass_cases: Caller has SIGINT = SIG_IGN: a child started by run() reports SIGINT ignored.
Caller has SIGINT = default_int_handler: a SIGINT during Popen is held and re-raised (test_f3).
After run() returns, the caller's SIGINT handler is what it was before (SIG_IGN stays SIG_IGN).
findings.summary: hold_stops replaces an ignored SIGINT with a handler during Popen, so the gate command now starts with SIGINT live instead of ignored

details: CONFIRMED by reading. Project rule label: "Python: every new or changed function has types". The rule sets no severity; correct today,
evidence: git diff master...HEAD -- lib/relay_gate.py: the hunk at @@ -316 is inside def run(worktree, args=(), environ=None, quick=False).
failing_case: run(worktree, args=(), environ=None, quick=False) had its body changed by 7a1a1a9 and has no annotations; popen_then_stop and
cleanup in tests/test_gate_stops.py:97,106 are new and untyped. The project's Python rule says every new or changed function has
types; it should read e.g. run(worktree: str, args: Sequence[str] = (), environ: Optional[Mapping[str, str]] = None,
quick: bool = False) -> tuple[int, str, list[str]].
fix_hint: Annotate run() and the two test helpers.
pass_cases: run() carries parameter and return annotations; the gate's type check stays green.
popen_then_stop(*args: Any, **kwargs: Any) -> subprocess.Popen[bytes] and cleanup() -> None annotated.
cmd_gate's call relay_gate.run(worktree, extra, quick=quick) still type-checks.
reason: Types added to run() and helpers (6838974); gate green.
findings.summary: Python rule (types on new or changed functions): run() was changed and is still untyped; the new test helpers are untyped
